queseq6-formula#84.en: Turn each root into its factor, opposite sign: −${C(m)} gives (x + ${C(m)}), and ${C(n)} gives (x − ${C(n)})

queseq6-formula#86.en: Multiply out and read off c: (${C(m)})(−${C(n)}) = ${C(cVal)}

queseq6-formula#89.en: build the brackets — do not try to remember a sum-and-product formula

queseq6-formula#90.en: Simultaneous equations (substitution method). Which equation do you make a variable the subject of?

queseq6-formula#91.en: The simpler one — usually the LINEAR equation

queseq6-formula#92.en: The quadratic one — it has more information

queseq6-formula#94.en: Either — it makes no difference to the work

queseq6-formula#95.en: Rearrange the LINEAR equation (least work, no squares), then substitute that expression into the other equation.

queseq6-formula#96.en: Pick the easy (linear) equation and make one variable the subject.

queseq6-formula#97.en: Making a variable the subject means getting it alone on one side

queseq6-formula#98.en: In the linear equation nothing is squared, so it comes out in one or two moves

queseq6-formula#99.en: Rearranging the quadratic would leave a root sign in your expression — much messier

queseq6-formula#100.en: so rearrange the LINEAR one and substitute it into the other

queseq6-formula#101.en: From ${C(a)}x − y = ${C(c)}, the tidy subject to take is…

queseq6-formula#106.en: y = ${C(a)}x − ${C(c)} (watch the signs as it crosses). Substituting this into the other equation leaves one variable.

queseq6-formula#107.en: Choose the variable with nothing attached to it — here that is the y

queseq6-formula#109.en: move the y across, move the number across

queseq6-formula#110.en: taking x instead would drag in a division by ${C(a)} for no reason

queseq6-formula#111.en: Linear + quadratic simultaneous equations: how many solution PAIRS can there be?

queseq6-formula#112.en: Up to two — and each answer must be paired with its partner value

queseq6-formula#115.en: None — a line and a parabola can't be solved together

queseq6-formula#116.en: Substituting the line into the quadratic gives a quadratic → up to two x-values, each with its own y. Write each as a coordinate pair (x ; y).

queseq6-formula#117.en: Substitute, solve the quadratic, back-substitute, pair up.

queseq6-formula#118.en: Substituting the line into the quadratic leaves one variable, in a quadratic equation

queseq6-formula#119.en: A quadratic gives at most two answers, so there are at most two x-values

queseq6-formula#120.en: Each x has its own y, so the answers come out as up to two pairs (x ; y)

queseq6-formula#121.en: picture it: a line can cut a parabola twice, touch it once, or miss it

queseq6-formula#122.en: Final answers to simultaneous equations should be written as coordinate pairs, e.g. (3 ; −3). True?

queseq6-formula#123.en: Each x belongs to a specific y.

queseq6-formula#124.en: True — each solution is a PAIR that works in both equations, so write them together: (3 ; −3).

queseq6-formula#125.en: A solution has to satisfy BOTH equations, which takes an x and its own matching y

queseq6-formula#126.en: Listing the x-values alone loses which y belongs to which x

queseq6-formula#127.en: ∴ true — write each solution as a pair, with a SEMICOLON: (3 ; −3)

queseq6-formula#128.en: the comma is the decimal separator

queseq6-formula#129.en: You solved x = ${C(x0)}. How do you find the matching y?

queseq6-formula#130.en: Substitute x = ${C(x0)} back into the SUBJECT expression (the linear equation)

queseq6-formula#134.en: Back-substitute into the linear equation (the easy one): e.g. y = ${C(a)}(${C(x0)}) − ${C(c)} = ${C(y0)}, giving the pair (${C(x0)} ; ${C(y0)}).

queseq6-formula#135.en: Go back to the LINEAR equation — it is the easy one, and it is already y = …

queseq6-formula#136.en: Put the x in, bracketed: y = ${C(a)}(${C(x0)}) − ${C(c)}
